title: August and the Cellar
premise: Pest controller Oscar Kavanagh is called to a farmhouse where something leaves human fingerprints in the flour, and he dismisses it as a prank until an excavation crew behind the property unearths a cellar door sealed from the inside. The house's surviving owner, elderly Maud Perrin, reveals that her family survived generations of the thing below by singing it a lullaby whose final verse was deliberately lost — and now the door is open, the song unfinished, and the creature is learning to wear the faces of the dead. As neighbors vanish and reappear wearing borrowed smiles, Oscar discovers the fingerprints belong to people who once tried to bargain with it. In the end, Oscar descends into the cellar to recover the last verse from the thing itself, learns that singing it dooms the singer to take the creature's place, and instead teaches the verse to the dying Maud, who sings herself into the dark willingly — sealing the door from the inside one final time, with Oscar left alive, remembering everything.
about_author: A. M. Whitlock is the pen name of a former rural building inspector who spent a decade documenting the basements and foundations of failing farmhouses across the Midwest. They write horror about what old structures remember, and live, deliberately, in a house with no cellar.

chapters.title: Fingerprints in the Flour
chapters.summary: Oscar Kavanagh, a skeptical pest controller, arrives at the Perrin farmhouse to investigate clawed baseboards and finds small, unmistakably human fingerprints pressed into a tin of flour — prints belonging to Maud Perrin's brother, dead forty years. Told from Oscar's wry, rational POV, the chapter establishes his disbelief as armor. The emotional beat is unease: professionalism cracking at the edges as he drives home past the excavation crew digging behind the barn.

chapters.title: The Door Sealed From Within
chapters.summary: The crew breaks through to a stone cellar door bolted shut on the inside, and Oscar — summoned back for 'the infestation' — watches them pry it open against Maud's screaming protests. From Oscar's POV, the chapter escalates: cold air breathing upward, tools going missing, a worker found smiling in the trench who swears he's never been happier. The emotional beat is dread overtaking denial, as Maud tells him about the song and the missing last verse.

chapters.title: The Borrowed Smiles
chapters.summary: Neighbors begin returning from walks wearing faces that don't quite fit, greeting Oscar by names only the dead should know, and Maud's health collapses as she tries to reconstruct the lost verse from childhood memory. Shifting between Oscar's POV and Maud's fragmented recollections, the chapter reveals the family bargain: each generation fed it a singer. The emotional beat is grief and complicity — survival exposed as a debt passed down, and Oscar realizing the fingerprints are signatures.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: With the thing wearing Maud's brother's face at her bedside, Oscar descends alone into the cellar and hears the complete song sung by every voice it has ever taken. He learns the truth: the final verse transfers the hunger to whoever sings it. Climax becomes sacrifice when he carries the verse back up and gives it to Maud, who chooses to sing herself into the dark, sealing the door from within. The resolution lands on Oscar alive, disbelieving no longer, carrying the memory like a scar.
